My research explores how pathogens move among wildlife, livestock, and
people — and how that knowledge can guide conservation and public
health decisions. I work at three overlapping scales: the
**pathogen**, the **host community**, and the **landscape**.

Below are the main stories that tie my work together. Each section
links to the paper. Figures from my Royal Society and Wiley papers
are reproduced under their original CC-BY licences; the mastitis
diagram is an original schematic I drew to summarise the 2019
*Preventive Veterinary Medicine* paper.

## SARS-CoV-2 in white-tailed deer — current postdoctoral work

At Penn State I'm analysing GPS movement data and contact networks
from white-tailed deer (*Odocoileus virginianus*) across Pennsylvania
and eight other U.S. states, in collaboration with USDA and USGS. The
question: can deer act as a reservoir for SARS-CoV-2, and if so, what
does that mean for spillback into people?

## Wild bovids, habitat, and infectious disease in Southeast Asia — my PhD

My doctoral work at Massey University asked a simple question with
surprisingly complex answers: *where* do Thailand's threatened wild
bovids still have suitable habitat, and *where* does that habitat
overlap with domestic cattle — creating places of shared pathogens?

Five bovid species still roam Thailand: **gaur** (*Bos gaurus*),
**banteng** (*Bos javanicus*), **wild water buffalo** (*Bubalus
arnee*), **mainland serow** (*Capricornis sumatraensis*) and
**Chinese goral** (*Naemorhedus griseus*). Their populations have
declined sharply under habitat fragmentation, hunting, and contact
with domestic livestock that share their grazing grounds and
pathogens.

### Mapping the habitat that remains

In Horpiencharoen *et al.* (**Royal Society Open Science, 2024**), I
built ecological niche models for all five species across 13 Asian
countries and showed that **over half of the suitable habitat for
these wild bovids lies outside protected areas** — meaning that
conservation has to happen on the working landscape, not just inside
reserves.

![Habitat suitability across the five wild bovid species of Southeast
Asia, from Horpiencharoen *et al.* (2024). Warmer colours indicate
higher predicted habitat suitability. © 2024 The Authors, CC-BY
(*R. Soc. Open Sci.* **11**, 240574).](images/habitat-suitability.png){fig-alt="Habitat suitability maps across Southeast Asia for five wild bovid species."}

### Layering species together — where the landscape holds many at once

Suitability for one species is useful. Suitability for *several*
species stacked together is what matters for designing conservation
corridors. Summing the per-species maps gives a **habitat-richness**
surface that flags the places where the most wild bovids could
coexist — and where protection and monitoring give the biggest
return.

![Habitat-richness map derived by stacking the five species-specific
suitability layers. Darker pixels are places predicted to be suitable
for more wild bovid species at once — the highest-priority corridors
for multi-species conservation. © 2024 The Authors, CC-BY.](images/habitat-richness.png){fig-alt="Habitat richness map of Southeast Asia showing overlapping suitability zones for multiple wild bovid species."}

[Read the paper → DOI 10.1098/rsos.240574](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.240574)

### Where wildlife and livestock collide: mapping pathogen-transmission risk

In Horpiencharoen *et al.* (**Conservation Science and Practice,
2025**), I overlaid those habitat-suitability maps with cattle
density to find the **interface zones** — landscapes where wild
bovids and domestic cattle are most likely to share pathogens.

The interface is dominated by **forest edges, cropland, and
unclassified forest**, and — strikingly — **Kuiburi National Park
alone holds 274 km² of high-risk area** for gaur and banteng. For
wild water buffalo the largest risk zone (126 km²) overlaps with
Huai Thabthan–Had Samran. These maps give conservation managers and
veterinary services specific, mappable places to focus surveillance
and mitigation.

![Figure 1 from Horpiencharoen *et al.* (2025) — Bivariate maps of
wild bovid habitat suitability (blue) against cattle density
(yellow); dark red pixels are the high-risk interface. © 2025 The
Authors, CC-BY (*Conservation Science and Practice*,
e70111).](images/research/bovid-risk-map.jpg){fig-alt="Bivariate risk maps of Thailand highlighting overlap of wild bovid habitat and cattle density for gaur, banteng, and wild water buffalo."}

[Read the paper → DOI 10.1111/csp2.70111](https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70111)

### What happens if disease actually crosses the fence?

A map tells you *where* pathogens could spill, but not *what that
would do to the population*. In Horpiencharoen *et al.* (**Journal of
the Royal Society Interface, 2024**), I built stochastic
compartmental models of a gaur population under six cattle-borne
diseases: **anthrax, bovine tuberculosis, haemorrhagic septicaemia,
lumpy skin disease, foot-and-mouth disease, and brucellosis.**

The key findings:

- **Chronic infections** (brucellosis, bTB) cause the greatest
  long-term damage. Frequency-dependent brucellosis drove gaur
  populations down by ~97 %, with extinction in 16 % of simulations.
- **Acute, high-fatality diseases** (anthrax) had surprisingly
  *small* effects — infected animals die quickly and "burn out" the
  outbreak.
- **Disease-free populations** grew by an average of 228 % over 100
  years — so healthy gaur can recover, if given the chance.

![Modelled gaur population dynamics over 100 years, with and without
each disease. Left column: single example stochastic simulations.
Right column: 100 stochastic simulations. Compartments shown are
susceptible (S), exposed (E), infected (I), recovered/immune (R) and
removed (M), plus total. From Horpiencharoen *et al.* (2024),
© The Authors, CC-BY
(*J. R. Soc. Interface* **21**, 20240278).](images/gaur-disease-dynamics.png){fig-alt="Grid of time-series plots showing modelled gaur population dynamics under anthrax, bTB, haemorrhagic septicaemia at two fatality levels, lumpy skin disease, foot-and-mouth disease, and brucellosis."}

The total-population view at the end of 100 years makes the ordering
of threats unmistakeable: the **chronic, density-dependent infections**
(brucellosis, bovine tuberculosis) hollow the population out over
decades, while the **acute high-fatality infections** burn through
quickly and rebound. Disease-free populations grow steadily — a
reminder that healthy gaur recover when given the chance.

![Projected gaur population sizes after 100 years under each disease
scenario, relative to the disease-free baseline. The separation between
chronic and acute disease effects is stark — brucellosis and bTB
dominate the long-term risk picture. © 2024 The Authors, CC-BY.](images/gaur-population-projection.png){fig-alt="Summary plot of predicted gaur population sizes after 100 years under each disease scenario, showing brucellosis and bovine tuberculosis causing the largest long-term declines."}

[Read the paper → DOI 10.1098/rsif.2024.0278](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2024.0278)

## Dairy cows & mastitis — finding the risk factors that matter

Before wild bovids, my MSc and early veterinary work focused on a
very different interface: **small-holder dairy farms in western
Thailand.** Clinical mastitis is a costly, chronic problem for these
farmers, and ordinary regression often hides the relationships
between farm practices, pathogens, and treatment outcomes.

```{=html}
<figure class="mastitis-fig">
<object data="images/research/western-thailand-map.svg" type="image/svg+xml" aria-label="Western Thailand study area"></object>
<figcaption>Sampling locations of 43 smallholder dairy farms across three central-western provinces — Kanchanaburi, Ratchaburi, and Nakhon Pathom — with the sampled districts shaded on the inset. From Horpiencharoen <em>et al.</em> (2019), <em>Preventive Veterinary Medicine</em> <strong>164</strong>, 49–55 (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.prevetmed.2019.01.014">DOI</a>).</figcaption>
</figure>
```

In Horpiencharoen *et al.* (**Preventive Veterinary Medicine, 2019**),
my co-authors and I sampled 100 quarters of milk from 100 cows across
43 dairies and built a **Bayesian network** that connects farm
management (floor type, dry-cow therapy, milking-machine hygiene,
parity) to the pathogens isolated in mastitis milk (*Streptococcus*,
*Staphylococcus*, *E. coli*, *S. dysgalactiae*) and to antimicrobial
susceptibility (penicillin, gentamicin, cloxacillin, AMC).

The network made two things visible that ordinary statistics missed:

- **Concrete or rubber floors, hand stripping after machine milking,
  dry-cow therapy, and routine milking-machine cleaning** were the
  four strongest levers for reducing *Streptococcus* spp. — the
  dominant pathogen.
- **Most isolates were resistant to penicillin G (40 %),** but
  susceptible to **amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (81 %) and
  cloxacillin (64 %)** — useful, concrete guidance for farmers'
  first-line treatment.

```{=html}
<figure class="mastitis-fig">
<object data="images/research/mastitis-bayesian-network.svg" type="image/svg+xml" aria-label="Hand-drawn Bayesian network summarising the 2019 mastitis study"></object>
<figcaption>Original schematic summarising the Bayesian network in Horpiencharoen <em>et al.</em> (2019): farm-management practices (slate-blue) → milk pathogens (ivory) → clinical signs (sage) and antimicrobial susceptibility (taupe). Redrawn by the author for this site. Source: <em>Preventive Veterinary Medicine</em> <strong>164</strong>, 49–55 (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.prevetmed.2019.01.014">DOI 10.1016/j.prevetmed.2019.01.014</a>).</figcaption>
</figure>
```

## Spatial & computational epidemiology

I use spatial methods and reproducible workflows to bring ecology
into epidemiology (and vice-versa):

- Species distribution and habitat-suitability modelling.
- Spatial and spatiotemporal risk mapping for zoonotic disease.
- Stochastic compartmental models for wildlife populations.
- Open code and version control (R + GitHub) for every analysis.

See the [publications](publications.qmd) page for the full list.
